title: Cześć czy dzień dobry?
title_en: Formal and casual, side by side
note: C1 Block 9, unit 5 (spine O7, B2-SPINE inbox item 22). SITUATIONS GENRE, ZERO NEW LEMMAS - every word on every screen is already owned, and check_new.py was run over all of them. What is new is a DECISION, and it is registered as the structure register_switch: English says you to everyone, Polish makes you choose before you reach the verb. THE ONE HONEST FACT, and the reason the unit is worth a slot: FORMAL POLISH IS NOT A DIFFERENT WORD FOR you - IT IS A DIFFERENT PERSON OF THE VERB. Masz czas? is second person; Czy ma pan czas? is THIRD person with pan standing where a name would. Nothing in the course had said this: b1_polite shipped Czy moglby pan mi pomoc? as a frozen chunk and a2_ordering_func shipped Co pan poleca? as an opaque one, both deliberately unanalysed. This unit opens the pattern on verbs the learner has conjugated since A1 (ma, mieszka, robi, pracuje), so it costs zero new forms and turns two frozen chunks into a system - the dziekuje / ktorej / nowego chunk-to-slot treatment, fourth register. THE CONDITIONAL IS RE-READ, NOT RE-TAUGHT: b1_conditional_sg's chcialbym was glossed as politeness and is named here as what it actually is, a register move on chce with the same meaning. MOGLBY QUARANTINE HELD, and deliberately: Czy moglby pan mi pomoc? and Czy moglaby pani mi pomoc? are recycled WHOLE from b1_polite, no conditional of moc is derived, no new person is shown, and the one Pisanie item touching that frame blanks pomoc rather than moglby - the same conservative fork b1_vocative_chunks took. THE VOCATIVE IS NOWHERE: no Prosze pana / Prosze pani (pana is NEW anyway), no address forms, no seventh case - c1_vocative_note is four nodes later and R5 gives it the first mention. FENCED, all verified NEW: pana, panu, dobranoc, dzieki, witam, pozdrawiam, panstwo, and the whole written register - the written/spoken split as a SYSTEM is spine O12's permanent refusal and this unit takes only the spoken half. SYNONYM RULE (C1 batch 17) APPLIED: no Kontrola item offers Czesc beside Dzien dobry in a situation where both would pass. Every greeting item names a situation where the other choice is genuinely marked, and the two items where it is a matter of degree rather than of grammar say so in their explain string rather than pretending otherwise. DISTRACTORS are person-mixing (Czy masz pan czas?), gender errors (pani to a man) and register errors - all real taught Polish in the wrong slot, no fabricated non-words. NO CASE GOVERNOR ADDED; data/case-map.json unchanged.

intro.title: English says you to everybody. Polish makes you choose first.
intro.body:
There is no neutral you in Polish. Before you reach the verb you have already decided how you are addressing the person, and the decision shows in every sentence you say to them.

Casual is ty — the second-person verb you have used since A1, with the pronoun itself almost always left out.

Formal is pan to a man and pani to a woman. English has nothing corresponding; the nearest thing is the difference between calling somebody by their first name and calling them sir.

This unit teaches no new words. Every form on every slide is one you already own. What is new is knowing which of the two sets to reach for.

intro.title: Formal Polish is not a different word for you. It is a different person of the verb.
intro.body:
This is the fact the course has been holding back, and it is the whole unit.

When you address somebody as pan or pani, the verb goes into the THIRD person — the same form you use for he and she. pan is standing where a name would stand. Czy ma pan czas? is, word for word, does the gentleman have time.

So you need no new verb forms at all. You have had ma, mieszka, robi and pracuje since A1 as third-person forms; formal address simply puts them to a different use.

Two sentences you have known as frozen pieces turn out to be built this way: Czy mógłby pan mi pomóc? and Co pan poleca?

intro.title: The same errand, said both ways
intro.body:
Nothing here is new. It is the material you already have, sorted by which of the two sets it belongs to.

Read down the formal column: it is the language of a counter, a surgery, an office — which is where you will hear it, and where it will be said to you.

Read down the casual column: family, friends, children, anyone who has invited you to.

intro.title: chcę and chciałbym are the same wish at two levels
intro.body:
You met chciałbym at B1 and it was called polite. That was true but incomplete. It is a register move, not a softer meaning — the wish is identical and only the level changes.

The same is true of możesz against czy mógłby pan. Polish reaches for the conditional where English reaches for could rather than can, and it does it much more readily.

One consequence worth having: Chcę kawę at a counter is not rude in the way it would be in English, but it does mark you as either very familiar or a foreigner. Poproszę o kawę is what is actually said.

intro.title: Which to use, and what happens if you get it wrong
intro.body:
pan and pani with anyone you do not know, and with everybody at a counter, in an office, at the doctor's — whatever their age. ty with family, with friends, with children, and with anyone who has moved to ty first.

When you are not sure, use pan or pani. Being too formal in Polish reads as slightly stiff and nothing worse. Being too casual reads as a claim on the other person that you have not earned, and that one is heard.

The other direction matters just as much: you will be addressed as pan constantly, and a question aimed at you will arrive in the third person. Czy ma pan skierowanie? is being asked of you, not about somebody else.

quiz.prompt: You walk into the doctor's surgery →
quiz.explain: Cześć claims a familiarity you do not have with the receptionist. Dzień dobry is what everyone says walking in.
Dzień dobry to your own brother is not wrong Polish — it is a joke, and it would be heard as one.
Na razie is the casual half of the same pair — right for a friend, too easy for a counter.

quiz.prompt: Have you got time? — to a man you don't know →
quiz.explain: pan takes the third person, so ma and not masz. Czy masz pan czas? mixes the two registers inside one sentence.

quiz.prompt: Have you got time? — to a woman you don't know →
quiz.explain: Same third-person verb; only the word for the person changes with their gender.

quiz.prompt: Have you got time? — to your sister →
quiz.explain: Second person, and the pronoun ty is left out as always. Ma czas? without pan or pani would be asking about somebody else.

quiz.prompt: Where do you live? — to a man you don't know →
quiz.explain: mieszka is the form you already use for he lives. Formal address is that form, with pan standing where the name would.

quiz.prompt: What are you doing? — to a child →
quiz.explain: Children are addressed as ty. Using pan to a child would be heard as sarcasm.

quiz.prompt: Could you help me? — to a woman at a counter →
quiz.explain: pani goes with mogłaby, pan with mógłby — the two halves have to agree with each other.
Chcę kawę is not rude the way I want a coffee is in English, but it is not what is said at a counter.

quiz.prompt: The raised form of Chcę kawę, a man speaking →
quiz.explain: Same wish, higher register. The -bym ending is the man's form; a woman says chciałabym.

quiz.prompt: A receptionist is asking YOU whether you have a referral →
quiz.explain: This is the direction that catches people out: a third-person verb plus pan is aimed straight at you. Czy ma skierowanie? without pan would be asking about somebody else.
